walkthroughs.body_html:
Ecological Relationships — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Ecological Relationships brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Ecological Relationships.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division

mcqs.q: In osmosis, which direction does water move?
options: Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.
Water moves towards the sugar because sugar attracts water molecules chemically.
From a region of higher water potential (less concentrated solution) to lower water potential.
Water moves from high solute concentration to low solute concentration.

mcqs.q: During an action potential, do Na+ and K+ move through the same channels?
options: No — voltage-gated Na+ channels open first (depolarisation, Na+ in), then voltage-gated K+ channels open (repolarisation, K+ out).
Na+ and K+ swap places through the same channel at the same time.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.

mcqs.q: What makes antibodies effective against pathogens?
options: Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.
Water moves towards the sugar because sugar attracts water molecules chemically.
Antibodies are general-purpose proteins that work against any pathogen.
They have a specific shape complementary to antigens on a particular pathogen, marking it for destruction or neutralising it.

The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

mcqs.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. How many fit end-to-end across a 1 mm gap?
options: 500 bacteria
750 bacteria
250 bacteria
400 bacteria

mcqs.q: A student uses quadrats placed randomly to estimate the number of daisies in a field. Why are the quadrats placed randomly?
options: To avoid bias and give a representative sample
To make sure all daisies are counted exactly
To find the largest daisies only
To change the independent variable

mcqs.q: In a food chain: grass → rabbit → fox, what do the arrows represent?
options: The direction of energy and biomass transfer
The direction the animals move
Which organism is the largest
The flow of carbon dioxide

mcqs.q: If the number of foxes (predators) falls sharply, what is the most likely short-term effect on the rabbit population?
options: The rabbit population increases.
The rabbit population immediately dies out.
The rabbit population stays exactly the same forever.
Rabbits turn into producers.

mcqs.q: Why is only about 10% of energy passed to the next trophic level in a food chain?
options: Most energy is lost through respiration, movement and heat.
Energy is created at each level.
Predators refuse to eat 90% of their prey.
Energy is stored permanently and never used.
